lessons.title: Reading a CI pipeline: triggers, jobs, steps, artifacts
lessons.objective: Read .github/workflows/ci.yml and .gitlab-ci.yml fluently — two dialects describing the same quality-and-test pipeline.

blocks.text:
Two files describe the same automation in two dialects.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` (GitHub Actions): `on:` triggers (push to `main`, every `pull_request`) → one job `quality-and-test` on `ubuntu-latest` with `timeout-minutes: 10` → sequential **steps**.

`.gitlab-ci.yml` (GitLab): `default: image: python:3.12-bookworm` → **stages** (`quality`, `test`) → jobs grouped by stage.

Both end identically: everything under `evidence/` is uploaded **unconditionally** — `if: always()` on GitHub, `artifacts: when: always` on GitLab.
blocks.more: Anatomy worth memorizing: the trigger (`on:` / implicit) decides *when* the pipeline runs; the runner image (`runs-on: ubuntu-latest`, `image: python:3.12-bookworm`) decides *where*; `timeout-minutes: 10` bounds a hung job so a stuck test cannot burn runner hours forever. GitHub steps execute in order and a nonzero exit aborts the job — unless a step opts out with `if: always()`. GitLab's `artifacts:reports:junit` goes further than storage: GitLab parses `evidence/junit/test-results.xml` and renders per-test results in the merge-request UI. GitHub's `if-no-files-found: error` makes *missing* evidence itself a pipeline failure — silence is not allowed to pass.

blocks.question: In ci.yml, the 'Run tests' step exits nonzero. What happens to the 'Upload evidence' step that follows it?
options: It is skipped — a failed step aborts the rest of the job
It runs anyway — the step carries if: always()
The whole job retries from the top
It runs only on the main branch
blocks.reveal: Ordinarily a failed step aborts the job, but `if: always()` overrides the default condition for exactly this step. The JUnit XML and logs upload even on a red run — which is precisely when you need to download them.

blocks.instructions:
Open both pipeline files and trace them against each other:

```code .github/workflows/ci.yml .gitlab-ci.yml
```

In `ci.yml`, find: the `on:` triggers, `runs-on`, `timeout-minutes`, the lint/format/typecheck/test steps, and the `if: always()` on the upload step. In `.gitlab-ci.yml`, find `stages:`, the `default: image:`, `artifacts: when: always` in `default:`, and the job-level `artifacts:reports:junit`. For each GitHub construct, name the GitLab line that expresses the same thing (and note what only one of them does, e.g. `timeout-minutes`).

blocks.description: Checks that ci.yml really contains the unconditional evidence upload and the JUnit-producing test step you just read.

args.success_note: ci.yml confirmed: tests write JUnit XML and the upload-artifact step runs if: always() — evidence survives a red run.

blocks.question: Why does the artifact-upload step use if: always() instead of the default condition?
options: So the pipeline finishes faster by skipping dependency checks
Because upload-artifact@v4 requires an explicit condition
So evidence uploads even when tests fail — a failing run is exactly when the JUnit XML and logs are needed for diagnosis
So the artifact is retained longer than the default 90 days
blocks.explanation: The default step condition is success() — it only runs if everything before it passed. A red test run is the one case where the evidence is indispensable, so the upload must be unconditional. The same idea appears in GitLab as `artifacts: when: always`.

blocks.question: GitHub stores the artifact as a zip download; GitLab does something more with the JUnit file. Which GitLab key is that, and what does it buy you?
blocks.sample_answer: `artifacts:reports:junit: evidence/junit/test-results.xml` tells GitLab to parse the JUnit XML as a test report, so per-test pass/fail results render directly in the merge-request UI instead of requiring an artifact download.

hints.text: Both files answer the same five questions: when does it run, where does it run, what does it run, how long may it take, and what survives the run.
In ci.yml read the `on:` block, the `quality-and-test` job, and the last step. In .gitlab-ci.yml read `default:`, `stages:`, and the `test` job's `artifacts:` block.

GitHub step condition `if: always()` (ci.yml, Upload evidence step) = GitLab `artifacts: when: always` (default block). GitLab-only extra: `artifacts:reports:junit` turns the XML into a rendered test report.

lessons.title: The gate chain: ruff, format, mypy, pytest
lessons.objective: Run the four CI quality gates locally, exactly as CI runs them, and internalize the nonzero-exit contract each one enforces.

blocks.text:
CI enforces a **gate chain**. Every tool honors the same contract: exit 0 means pass, anything nonzero fails the job.

1. `ruff check src simulator tests learning` — lint
2. `ruff format --check src simulator tests learning` — formatting, check-only: it reports, never rewrites
3. `mypy src simulator learning` — strict type checking
4. `pytest` — the suite itself

The order is deliberate: cheapest and fastest first. A lint failure in seconds saves the minutes a full test run would have burned.
blocks.more: The configurations live in `pyproject.toml`, so local and CI runs share one source of truth: ruff's line length and lint rules, mypy's `strict = true`, pytest's `--strict-markers`. That is what makes "run the same commands locally" meaningful — you are not approximating CI, you are executing it. `--check` on `ruff format` is the read-only twin of `ruff format`: it exits 1 and lists files it *would* reformat, without touching them. GitHub runs the four as separate steps (you see which gate failed at a glance); GitLab chains them in one `script:` list (first failure aborts the rest). Same gates, different granularity.

blocks.question: ruff format --check prints "1 file would be reformatted" and exits 1. Did it modify the file?
options: Yes — that is how ruff enforces formatting
No — --check is read-only; only plain `ruff format` rewrites
Yes, but only files under src/
blocks.reveal: --check turns the formatter into a pure verifier: nonzero exit and a report, zero writes. In CI that is exactly what you want — the pipeline judges, it does not edit. Locally, `ruff format src simulator tests learning` is the fix.

blocks.instructions:
Run the full gate chain locally, exactly as CI does (repo root, venv active):

```ruff check src simulator tests learning
ruff format --check src simulator tests learning
mypy src simulator learning
python -m pytest
```

All four must exit 0. If any gate fails, fix what it reports and rerun it before moving on — that loop is the point of the exercise.
blocks.command: ruff check src simulator tests learning

blocks.description: Runs the first gate (ruff check) in a subprocess from the repo root and requires the exit code to be 0 — the same contract CI enforces.

args.snippet:
import subprocess, sys
r = subprocess.run([sys.executable, '-m', 'ruff', 'check', 'src', 'simulator', 'tests', 'learning'], capture_output=True)
print('ruff exit:', r.returncode)
args.success_note: ruff check exits 0 on src, simulator, tests, and learning — the first gate is green locally, exactly as CI will run it.

blocks.question: CI will run all four gates anyway. Why run the identical chain locally before pushing?
blocks.sample_answer: Local runs give feedback in seconds without spending CI minutes or publishing a red commit for the team to see. Because pyproject.toml makes the local and CI configurations identical, a locally green chain almost never fails remotely — CI becomes a confirmation, not a discovery.

hints.text: Each gate is a process with the same contract you saw in the main() lesson: exit 0 or the job goes red. Nothing else about them is magic.
The exact four commands are the `run:` lines of the Lint / Check formatting / Type check / Run tests steps in .github/workflows/ci.yml — copy them verbatim.
Check a gate's exit code after each run: `echo $LASTEXITCODE` in PowerShell (`echo $?` in bash). If ruff format --check complains, `ruff format src simulator tests learning` applies the fix.

lessons.title: A controlled failure: evidence when the test goes red
lessons.objective: Inject a deliberate test failure, capture its JUnit evidence, and connect the red exit code to the unconditional artifact upload from the pipeline.

blocks.text:
A failing test is when evidence matters most — and pytest keeps collecting it. The assertion fails, pytest records a `<failure>` node (with the message) inside the testcase in the JUnit XML, writes the file anyway, and exits 1.

In CI, that exit 1 turns the job red, and the `if: always()` upload step from the first lesson still ships the XML. Red run, intact evidence.

You will now inject that failure **on purpose**, tagged with a requirement marker, and read the evidence it leaves behind.
blocks.more: pytest exit codes are a small vocabulary: 0 = all passed, 1 = tests ran and some failed, 2 = interrupted, 5 = no tests collected. CI only distinguishes zero/nonzero, but you will see these in logs. The JUnit `<failure>` node carries the assertion message in its `message` attribute and the traceback as its text — that is what GitLab renders via `artifacts:reports:junit` and what you download from GitHub's `test-evidence` artifact. The `@pytest.mark.requirement(...)` marker is registered in pyproject.toml (`--strict-markers` is on, so an unregistered marker would itself be an error); it is what ties a red testcase back to the requirement it verifies.

blocks.question: You run pytest on a failing test with --junitxml=evidence/exercises/results.xml. What is the exit code, and does results.xml get written?
options: Exit 1, and results.xml is written containing a <failure> node
Exit 1, so results.xml is not written
Exit 2, because the test is outside the tests/ directory
blocks.reveal: Test failures are exit 1 — and writing the JUnit report is part of pytest's job regardless of outcome. An explicit nodeid overrides the configured testpaths, so a file under evidence/exercises/ runs fine.

blocks.instructions:
Create `evidence/exercises/test_controlled_failure.py` with one deliberately failing test marked `@pytest.mark.requirement("REQ-LEARN-002")` (hint level 3 has the exact content). Then run it and capture the report:

```New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force evidence\exercises   # PowerShell; bash: mkdir -p evidence/exercises
python -m pytest evidence/exercises/test_controlled_failure.py --junitxml=evidence/exercises/results.xml
echo $LASTEXITCODE   # PowerShell; bash: echo $?
```

Confirm the exit code is 1. Then open `evidence/exercises/results.xml`, find the `<testcase>` for `test_controlled_failure`, and read the `<failure>` node — its `message` attribute should carry your injected message.

blocks.description: Re-runs your controlled failure in a sandboxed evidence directory and requires pytest to exit nonzero with the testcase present in the JUnit report — proving the failure and its evidence are both real.
Checks that your own results.xml — the file you produced, not the sandbox's — parses as JUnit XML and contains the failed testcase.

args.success_note: results.xml records test_controlled_failure as a <failure>, not merely as a name — the red run left durable, parseable evidence, exactly as it would inside a CI artifact.

blocks.question: If this failing test ran inside the GitHub Actions job, which step configuration guarantees the evidence would survive the red test — and why?
blocks.sample_answer: The upload-artifact step carries `if: always()`, so it executes even though the test step exited nonzero. The JUnit XML with the <failure> node is uploaded in the test-evidence artifact either way — the failing run is precisely the one you need to download.

hints.text: pytest does not stop at the assertion — it records it. Think about where the record goes (the --junitxml file) and what exit code CI will see.

The marker is registered in pyproject.toml under [tool.pytest.ini_options] markers as requirement(identifier). --strict-markers is active, so spell it exactly: @pytest.mark.requirement("REQ-LEARN-002").
After the run, results.xml should contain a line like: <failure message="injected failure for evidence study"> — search the file for '<failure' to jump straight to it.
